little.twist: Mo has two problems, and Robo needs two steps in one go.
little.can_now: listen to someone who is upset, say sorry and fix it, and give clear instructions

steps.say: Market day at your stall! Here comes Mo. Oh: he looks cross.
What do you do first?

choices.why: When someone is upset, listen first. Then they feel heard.
Walking away leaves the problem. Stay, look at Mo and listen.

steps.done: You looked at Mo and listened. He feels heard.

steps.say: Mo says: "{gripe}"
Show Mo you listened. What do you say?

choices.why: Blaming makes people crosser. Saying it back shows you listened.
That doesn't show you listened. Say back what happened.

steps.done: Mo nods: you understood him.

steps.say: Now say sorry.

choices.why: That sounds as if you don't care. A real sorry helps.
A 'but' takes the sorry away. Just say sorry.

steps.done: A kind sorry. Mo feels better.

steps.say: Fix it: give Mo a fresh loaf. Touch the bread.
steps.done: A fresh loaf for Mo!

steps.say: Mo says: "And the lid of my jam was loose!" Fix that too: touch the jam.
steps.done: A new jar of jam, with its lid on tight.

steps.say: Mo smiles. What do you say now?

choices.why: Mo helped you by telling you. Thank him, and he'll come back.
A thank you shows you're glad he told you.

steps.done: Mo says he'll come back tomorrow.

steps.say: Robo the robot helps you tidy up. Robo does EXACTLY what you say, so say it clearly!
The red box goes in the basket. What do you tell Robo?

choices.text: "Robo, put the red box in the basket."

choices.why: Robo did exactly that: something, somewhere! 'It' and 'there' could be anything. Say which box, and where.
Robo spun round: 'the thing' could be anything. Say what to do.

steps.done: Robo put the red box in the basket. Clear words!

steps.say: Now the blue box goes on the table.

choices.text: "Robo, put the blue box on the table."

choices.why: Robo said "Blue!" back. Say what to do with it, and where.
Robo tidied himself into the basket! Say which box goes where.

steps.done: The blue box is on the table. Robo beeps happily.

steps.say: The yellow box goes on top of the red one. Two steps in one go: what do you say?

choices.text: "Robo, pick up the yellow box, then put it on the red box."

choices.why: Robo is muddled: say each step, in order.
Robo stacked everything, even his own feet! Say which box goes where.

steps.done: Yellow on red: Robo did both steps, in order.

steps.say: Pip-pop has a ball. You'd like a turn. How do you ask?

choices.why: That sounds bossy. A question and a please work better.
Grabbing isn't fair. Ask, and wait for your turn.

steps.done: Pip-pop says: "Yes! Your turn next."

steps.say: You listened, said sorry, fixed it and gave clear words. That's how good talkers do it!

check.say: Someone is upset with you. What do you do first?
Which one is a good sorry?
Robo does exactly what you say. Which words are clear?

choices.text: "Put the red box in the basket."

check.say: How do you ask for a turn?

name_it.title: Talk like a pro
lines: Look at the person, and listen first.
Say sorry, and fix it if you can.
Clear words: what, which and where.
name_it.source: CASEL's relationship skills (communicate clearly, listen actively) and the EU's EntreComp (working with others)

little.try_real: With a grown-up: play Robo. One of you gives instructions to make a sandwich, and the other does EXACTLY what is said.

sources.fact: Relationship skills: communicating clearly, listening actively, cooperating, solving conflicts well and asking for or offering help.
Children's social skills at five predict education, work and staying out of trouble as young adults.
sources.source: Jones, Greenberg and Crowley (2015), American Journal of Public Health 105(11)

sources.fact: Working with others and communicating are part of turning ideas into value for others.
sources.source: EntreComp, the EU's Entrepreneurship Competence Framework (2016)

middle.twist: Ana can only spare half a crate: can you still find a win-win?
middle.can_now: ask what the other person needs, make a fair win-win deal and keep the promise

steps.say: Your stall needs apples for apple cake. Ana the farmer has apples. Let's make a deal that's good for both of you.
Before you offer anything, find out what Ana wants. What do you ask?

choices.text: "What do you need most this week?"

choices.why: That only thinks of you. Ask what she needs: then you can help each other.
That's an order, not a deal. Ask first.

steps.done: A good question: now you know what she needs.

steps.say: Ana says: "I need bread for my helpers at harvest time. And my crates are so heavy!"
What is a win-win offer?

choices.text: "4 loaves for a crate of apples, and I'll help you carry."

choices.why: That's not fair for Ana. She'd say no, and she wouldn't trust you next time.
'One day' isn't a deal. Say what you'll give, and when.

steps.done: Ana smiles: "That works for both of us!"

steps.say: Ana says: "I can only spare half a crate this week." What now?

choices.text: "Half a crate for 2 loaves, and I'll help carry your crates."
"Then give me the whole crate anyway."
choices.why: She can't, so that's no deal. Find what you can both do.
Don't give up too fast: a smaller deal can still be win-win.

steps.done: A smaller deal, still good for both of you.

steps.say: Shake hands on the deal: hold Ana's hand.
steps.done: It's a deal!

steps.say: You said you'd bring the bread on Friday. On Friday you're very busy. What do you do?

choices.text: Bring it anyway, or tell Ana early and agree a new time
Forget it: they were only words
choices.why: A promise is a deal. Keeping it is how people come to trust you.
Hiding makes it worse. Tell her early and agree a new time.

steps.done: That's someone people can count on.

steps.say: Friday: keep your promise. Put the bread in Ana's basket.
steps.done: Promise kept! Ana trusts you more.

steps.say: Robo is helping you tidy the stall. Remember: Robo does EXACTLY what you say.
The apples go in the blue crate, under the table. What do you say?

choices.text: "Robo, put the apples in the blue crate under the table."

choices.why: Robo put them... away! Where? Say what, and exactly where.
Robo is muddled: say it as one whole, clear sentence.

steps.done: Apples in the blue crate, under the table. Exactly right.

steps.say: Robo must fetch the yellow box: it's ahead, then to his left. Give him the steps in order: touch the cards.
steps.done: FORWARD, TURN LEFT, PICK UP: Robo did it, step by step.

steps.say: A customer says: "Your apple cake was {cake_gripe}." What do you do?

choices.text: Listen, say sorry, offer a fresh slice and thank them

choices.why: Listen first: a complaint is free advice to make things better.
Ignoring it loses a customer. Listen, say sorry and fix it.

steps.done: The customer says: "Thank you! I'll come again."

steps.say: You asked what Ana needed, made a win-win deal, kept your promise and gave clear steps. Well done!

check.say: Before you make a deal, you...

choices.text: ask what the other person needs

check.say: You made a promise, and now you can't keep it. You...

choices.text: tell them early and agree a new time
"Put the apples in the blue crate under the table."

name_it.title: A win-win deal
lines: Ask what the other person needs.
Make a fair offer that helps you both.
Shake on it, and keep your promise.
Clear instructions: what, which, where, in order.
name_it.source: The Harvard Program on Negotiation (interests, not positions; from Getting to Yes) and CASEL's relationship skills

middle.try_real: With a grown-up: plan a fair swap with a friend or a brother or sister (a toy, a turn, a job), where you both get something you want.

sources.fact: Understanding the other side's interests leads to agreements that satisfy each side's interests.
sources.source: Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School: BATNA and interests (after Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes)

sources.fact: Relationship skills include communicating clearly, listening actively and negotiating conflict constructively.
Working with others and mobilising resources are entrepreneurship competences.

big.twist: A tricky numbers question, and a 'sign now' offer.
big.can_now: pitch an idea (the problem, the idea, why me, what I need), take feedback and say no to an unfair deal

steps.say: You want a bread cart to sell at the Launch Site. Three friendly investors will listen to your pitch. Stand tall, smile and speak clearly.
A strong pitch has four parts. Touch them in order on your pitch board: the PROBLEM, your IDEA, WHY YOU, WHAT YOU NEED.
steps.done: That's the order of a strong pitch.

steps.say: First, the PROBLEM. Say it so they can picture it:

choices.text: "The builders at the Launch Site walk 20 minutes to buy lunch."

choices.why: True, but what's the problem? Say who needs something, and why.
Investors want to hear what people need, not what you want.

steps.done: Mr Diaz nods: he can picture it.

steps.say: Now your IDEA:

choices.text: "A bread cart that comes to the Launch Site at lunchtime."
"A bakery on the Moon, by Tuesday!"
choices.why: Exciting, but can you really do it? Investors trust ideas you can do.
Be clear: what exactly is your idea?

steps.done: A clear idea that fixes the problem.

steps.say: WHY YOU?

choices.text: "I ran my stall for two weeks, and customers came back."
"I'm the best baker in the world."
choices.why: Show it, don't boast: say what you have done.
Wanting is a start. What have you done that shows you can?

steps.done: Facts they can check: that builds trust.

steps.say: WHAT YOU NEED:

choices.text: "50 coins for a cart. You get 1 coin of every 10 it makes, for a year."

choices.why: How much, and what for? Give a clear number, and say what they get.
Ask for what the idea really needs, and say what they get back.

steps.done: A clear ask, and what they get back.

steps.say: Look at each investor as you speak: one, two, three. Touch each one.
steps.done: Good eye contact: they feel you're talking to them.

steps.say: Mr Diaz asks: "What if it rains?"

choices.text: "Good question! I'll put a cover on the cart and test it in the first week."

choices.why: Making things up loses trust. Say what you'll do, or that you'll find out.
Every question is a chance to show you've thought about it.

steps.done: An honest answer with a plan.

steps.say: Mr Diaz asks: "You make 2 coins on each loaf. How many loaves pay back the 50 coins?"

choices.why: Each loaf makes 2 coins, so 50 ÷ 2 = 25 loaves.

choices.text: "I don't know, and it doesn't matter."
choices.why: It's fine not to know at once, but say you'll work it out: the numbers matter.

steps.done: 25 loaves: you know your numbers.

steps.say: Ms Ade says: "Your price is a bit high for the builders."

choices.text: "Thank you. What price would feel fair to them?"

choices.why: Feedback is free advice. Listen, ask, then decide.
It's fine to feel a bit sad. Feedback helps you get better: ask about it.

steps.done: Ms Ade: "I like how you listen."

steps.say: Mrs Kowalski offers 50 coins, but she wants 9 of every 10 coins your cart makes, for ever.

choices.text: "Thank you, but no: that's not fair for the cart."

choices.why: Not every deal is a good deal. You can say no politely and keep looking.
Stay polite: you can say no kindly, and she may offer better later.

steps.done: A polite no. Mrs Kowalski nods: she respects that.

steps.say: Mrs Kowalski says: "Sign now, or the offer is gone for ever!"

choices.text: "I'll think it over, and talk to a grown-up first."

choices.why: 'Now or never' is a pressure trick. A fair offer can wait while you think.
Being polite doesn't mean saying yes. Take your time.

steps.done: Good: a fair offer can always wait while you think.

steps.say: Ms Ade offers 50 coins for 1 coin of every 10 the cart makes, for one year.

choices.text: "That's fair for both of us. Yes, please!"

choices.why: Investors need something back too. Fair for both is the best deal.
She's taking a risk on you, so a fair share back is right.

steps.done: Ms Ade comes round the table to shake on it.

steps.say: Shake hands with Ms Ade: hold her hand.
steps.done: Deal! Your bread cart is on its way.

steps.say: Pip-pop pitched her lemonade stand. Give her kind, useful feedback:

choices.text: "I liked your sign! Next time, say how much you need."

choices.why: Feedback should help: one thing you liked, and one thing to try.
Kind, but it doesn't help her get better. Add one thing to try.

steps.done: Pip-pop: "Thanks! I'll try that."

steps.say: A clear pitch, honest answers, a polite no and a fair deal. That's how founders talk!

check.say: An investor says your price is too high. You...

choices.text: thank them and ask what would be fair

check.say: An offer is unfair. You can...

choices.text: say no politely and keep looking

check.say: 'Sign now or it's gone for ever!' is...

choices.text: a pressure trick: take your time
one thing you liked, and one thing to try

name_it.title: Pitch, listen, deal fairly
lines: The problem, your idea, why you, what you need.
Look at your listeners and speak clearly.
Answer honestly: say when you'll find out.
Feedback is free advice: listen, then decide.
Say no politely to an unfair deal.
name_it.source: EntreComp (2016: mobilising others, working with others) and the Harvard Program on Negotiation (your best alternative)

big.try_real: With a grown-up: pitch an idea for something at home (a family game night, a garden patch) in four parts: the problem, the idea, why you, what you need.

sources.fact: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) is the measure of any deal: you can say no to a bad one.
sources.source: Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School

sources.fact: Mobilising others (inspire, persuade, communicate) and working with others are entrepreneurship competences; value for others can be financial, cultural or social.
Leadership and social influence are among the skills employers rank highest.
sources.source: World Economic Forum, The Future of Jobs Report 2025
